extracted.intended_audience: aspiring creative writers and memoirists; readers interested in 19th-century wartime/battlefield description
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing immersive, memoir-style battlefield and wartime scene descriptions that combine topographical mapping, concrete artifacts, personal anecdote, and moral reflection. Useful for creative writers aiming to evoke the scale, sensory reality, and human consequences of combat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground-and-configuration description
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the configuration of the ground and the position's strategic importance (ridges, hollows, roads, hills, approaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the terrain for the reader: name ridges, note distances (e.g., 'crest of each ridge is distant nearly a mile'), identify key features (cemetery, turnpike, Emmetsburg road, Round Hill) and explain how those features affected the battle (e.g., 'The hill... was the center of our line of battle and the key to our position'). Use spatial progression (center → left → extreme left) to organize the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete artifacts as evidentiary detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor scenes in specific, tangible objects found on the field (broken wheels, Testament in a tree, head-boards, muskets, cartridge-boxes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring the past to life by inventorying debris and personal items: broken gun-carriage wheel, exploded caisson, Testament with name, knapsack back nailed to a head-board. These small objects serve as evocative proof of events and personalize otherwise overwhelming destruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of numbers and scale to convey magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ concrete counts and comparative figures to communicate scale (men, horses, graves, ridges, miles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State numbers where known (e.g., 'twenty-seven dead horses', 'two thousand men', 'a population of four or five thousand') to give readers a quantitative sense of scale and loss. Juxtapose small figures and vast totals to dramatize outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory and visceral detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Include vivid sensory impressions—sight, smell, tactile evidence—of battle's aftermath (blood-drenched grass, decomposing horse, shattered garments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use graphic, specific sensory language to make the scene immediate: 'the grass is drenched in blood', 'body cut in two by a shell', 'faces swollen'. Balance shocking detail with restraint when appropriate to avoid gratuitousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple vantage points / guided walk
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the description as a walk or circuit that takes the reader through different viewpoints (cemetery → ridge → orchard → hollow → farm-house).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a moving narrator who progresses across the field, noting changes and discoveries at each stop. This produces a coherent narrative through-line and allows sequential revelations (artillery traces → graves → orchard → farmhouse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanization through personal effects and identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanize the dead and participants by pointing out identity markers and mundane personal effects (name on Testament, brass plate, knapsack, canteen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show identity or attempted identity-recovery by citing marked belongings. These details create empathy and individualize mass casualties ('Charles Durrale, Corporal of Company G' written on the fly-leaf).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anecdote and local color
rubrics_metrics.description: Interleave short anecdotes or local stories to reveal character, morale, and social consequences (e.g., the woman who cried because town was taken by 18 when 'we had a thousand that ran away').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, often humorous or ironic community anecdotes can relieve intensity and add human perspective. Place them to illuminate attitudes, civilian responses, or the absurdities of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative historical analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the present field with well-known historical battles or scenes to give weight and perspective (e.g., Waterloo, Wagram, Jena; Hougoumont at Waterloo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogy sparingly to situate the battle in a broader military-historical frame and to highlight contrasts (e.g., fertility after battle at Waterloo vs. ravaged fields at Gettysburg). Analogies create resonance and help readers relate unfamiliar details to known history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing with dated/reportage elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame narrative with dated telegrams, letters, or reportage cues to establish immediacy and eyewitness authority ('Report at Harrisburg...'; 'To-day I have passed along the whole ground...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open or intersperse first-person dated notes or reproduced dispatches to anchor the account in time and reportage. This conveys urgency and lends documentary authority to observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphoric and thematic closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use metaphor or emblematic phrasing to express thematic meaning (e.g., 'Another harvest, in which Death was the reaper').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a resonant metaphor at moments of summarization to translate concrete devastation into broader moral or poetic commentary. Avoid overwrought cliche; choose metaphors that grow naturally from the described scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of civilian and landscape consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict how battle altered civilian spaces (cemetery desecrated, farms cut up, schools/hospitals repurposed) and the social fallout (exiles, auctions, banishments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace the ripple effects beyond the battlefield: ruined cemeteries, repurposed seminaries as hospitals, auctioning of household goods, banishment of civilians. Showing these consequences broadens the scene's moral and social dimensions.
